stem: A 29-year-old woman who has grown up in Australia presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a rapidly growing mole on her left forearm. Biopsy demonstrates it to be a malignant melanoma. explanation: Melanoma thickness is stratified into four categories:≤1.0 mm,1.01-2.0 mm, 2.01-4.0mm and4.0 mm. Five-year survival rates in all four categories in the presence or absence of ulceration decrease progressively as thickness increases. Lesions less than 1mm are associated with a 95% 5-year survival,T4 lesions, (4mm in thickness) have a survival of approximately 20% at 5 years. Q.

explanation: Anti-Ro and La antibodies,found in adult patients with SLE, are associated with the development of neonatal complete heart block when found in pregnant women. Limited evidence supports continued use of hydroxychloroquinein pregnancy, and reduced SLE disease activity in the woman may in turn reduce Ro and La antibody titres, and hence neonatal symptoms of heart block. stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He is a keen sportsman, but has a history of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy in the family, thought to be related to a relatively rare mutation in a gene coding for actin. Where is actin found in cardiac muscle cell?
options: As a component of the thick filaments
As a component of the thin filaments
explanation: Actin, along with tropmyosin and troponin, is a component of the thin filaments of the cardiac myocyte. Actin is a globular protein arranged as a chain of repeating units which form two strands of an alpha helix. Tropomyosin interdigitates between the strands and troponin is attached to it.

stem: You are taking part in a clinical trial which is thought to modify the cellular make-up of unstable atherosclerotic plaques. Intravascular ultrasound suggests a reduction in the necrotic core because of a reduction in foam cells. Which cells make up most of the population of foam cells?

In patients who are immunocompetent, the disease is self-Limiting, with systemic features of infection resolving over a few days, and lymph nodes regressing in size over a period of 2-5 months. For this reason supportive therapy only, with antipyretics, is appropriate.

stem: A72-year-old man, who had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease some 5 years earlier, comes to the Emergency Department with severe nausea and vomiting, thought to be related to eating out-of-date chicken curry. He is unable to take his oral Parkinson's disease medications. On examination his BP is 130/90 mmHg lying and 100/75 mmHg standing. Pulse increases by 10 beats per minute on standing. His abdomen is soft, but there is general tenderness and bowel sounds are active. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 174×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 12.9 mmol/l 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Glucose 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L IV fluids are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate anti-emetic to reduce the likelihood of future vomiting?
explanation: Ondansetron is a highly potent 5HT3 receptor antagonist. It does not act as a dopamine antagonist and does not affect prolactin levels, and therefore represents the most appropriate intervention here. Although anti- emetics may not be considered in many cases of gastroenteritis, reducing vomiting willallow the patient to maintain oral therapy for Parkinson's in this situation. Alternatives to ondansetron include cyclizine and domperidone.

stem: A54-year-old man who owns a bar in Spain comes to the Emergency Department straight from the airport. He has a history of type 2 diabetes and stepped on a piece of glass whilst not wearing shoes some 2 weeks earlier. He is clutching an X-ray report from Spain which confirms there was no glass in the foot. He has peripheral neuropathy and only noticed the cut sometime later. On examination, his BP is 123/82 mmHg, pulse is 84 bpm and regular. His temperature is 37.7 ℃. There is a 3cm cut across the underside of his left foot, with surrounding swelling and erythema, and it is exuding pus.You immediately start him on co- amoxiclav. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129g/L 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 112 mg/L 0-10 mg/L HbA1c Which of the following is the most important investigation in this patient?
options: Microscopy, culture and sensitivity of pus
explanation: In this situation, the most important investigation to stratify the level of required intervention is MRI of the foot. After 2 weeks of symptoms, it's highly likely that changes on the MRI will be present in the event that the patient has osteomyelitis, and thus the scan is a driver for surgical debridement.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with primary pulmonary hypertension(PPH) comes to the clinic for review. She is currently taking bosentan but has suffered from worsening of her shortness of breath, decreased exercise tolerance, and ankle swelling over the past three months. Her BP is 132/82mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Chest is clear, JVP is elevated and there is pitting oedema of both ankles. A decision is made to start sildenafil. Which of the following correctly reflects the main mode of action of sildenafil?
explanation: Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor developed for the treatment of erectile dysfunction. Its vasodilatory properties led to clinical trials in patients with pulmonary hypertension, and it was found to be an effective adjunct to other therapies for the condition.

stem: A 19-year-old man attends the Emergency Department with his parents. They are very concerned about him as over the past few months he has become increasingly withdrawn, confining himself to his room for hours per day, and continuously smoking cannabis. Apparently he has also installed blackout blinds in his room which are permanently drawn. Apparently he has previously attended the department with both drug and alcohol abuse. You try and examine the patient but he refuses all but basic observations. He looks anxious and unkempt, with a long beard and clothes that haven't been changed for some days. He tells you the police are monitoring him, listening to all of his thoughts, and because a red van drives past his house at 5.30 pm each day he is under surveillance. What is his description of the red van?
explanation: The van passing at 5.30 pm is likely to be the post van, driving by to collect letters from a post box. The fact that this patient links the occurrence directly to his personal circumstances, suggests a delusion of reference due to underlying schizophrenia.

stem: You are reviewing a 54-year-old man who is taking isoniazid as part of triple therapy for tuberculosis infection. Which of the following fits best with the action of isoniazid?
explanation: lsoniazid inhibits bacterial fatty acid synthase. This inhibits the synthesis of mycolic acids, which are required components of the mycobacterial cell wall. It is bacteriocidal to rapidly growing mycobacteria.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of itching and irritation around the anal margin, particularly at night, for the past few weeks. She has no significant change in bowel habit and her two young children complain of the same features. She tells you that she noticed what looked like tiny pieces of string around the anal margin of her youngest child (aged 3) when she woke from sleep the previous evening. General physical examination is unremarkable, although you do note evidence of excoriation around the anus. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Albendazole followed 2-3 weeks later by a second dose
Itraconazole followed 2-3 weeks later by a second dose
Metronidazole followed 2-3 weeks later by a second dose
Mebendazole followed 2-3 weeks later by a second dose
Tinidazole followed 2-3 weeks later by a second dose
explanation: This is the drug of choice in adults and children aged above 2 years for the treatment of threadworms. Mebendazole kills live worms, not eggs, hence the dose is repeated after 2-3 weeks in case re-infection through unhatched eggs has occurred. To try to reduce the risk of re-infection, washing of bed sheets etc. is recommended, as is great attention to hand washing and reducing thumb sucking, nail biting etc.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes for the past 42 years comes to the Ophthalmology Clinic for review. She has relatively poor glycaemic control on a basal bolus insulin regimen, with a recent IFCC HbA1cmeasured at 69 mmol/mol. She smokes 10 cigarettes per day. Most recently she received pan retinal photocoagulation to her left eye for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, some 6 months ago. On examination her BP is 142/82mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Examination of the left eye reveals evidence of macular oedema. Which of the following is the most important next intervention for her sight?
explanation: Evidence supports the use of VEGF inhibitors in the treatment of diabetic maculopathy. Trials of both ranibizumab and bevacizumab suggest a higher complete regression rate for the group offered VEGF inhibitor on top of photcoagulation (88% versus 25% at 6 weeks for bevacizumab). Some regression of effect was seen for bevacizumab by week 16,although pegaptanib, another VEGF inhibitor, showed positive data out to week 36 with complete response(100% versus 25% for standard of care).

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic with a confirmed diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. He needs to start medication and you plan to initiate isoniazid, but he tells you he may have a liver problem which runs in the family. Which of the following represents the primary step in metabolism of isoniazid?
explanation: The primary step in metabolism of isoniazid is acetylation. Slow acetylation (i.e. defective action of N- acetyltransferase) is the genetic polymorphism present in 40-70% of Caucasians, and increases the risk of peripheral nerve toxicity with isoniazid therapy.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a 1-year history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for review. She is failing to gain control of her symptoms, has multiple joints affected by pain and swelling, and an increase in rheumatoid nodules affecting both elbows. There is increasing tiredness and she is currently unable to function adequately at work. Current medication includes methotrexate and naproxen. You elect to start her on etanercept. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of etanercept?
options: Binds to the TNF receptor and circulating TNF
explanation: Etanercept is a competitive inhibitor of TNF binding to its cell surface receptors, and thereby inhibits the biological activity of TNF.TNF is a pro-inflammatory cytokine thought to be closely involved in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A21-year-old man with a history of type 1 diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with severe nausea and vomiting, a fever and cough productive of purulent sputum. Despite increasing his insulin dose by 50%, he is unable to maintain blood glucose control. On examination his BP is 100/80 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular. There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation of the chest, abdomen is soft with some epigastric tenderness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 299×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 37.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L* Bicarbonate(HCO) 14 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Urine ketones Which of the following is the main ketoacid likely to be present in this patient?
explanation: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is formed by the reduction of acetoacetic acid, and is the only true ketoacid formed in diabetic ketoacidosis. It can be measured directly in serum, and by introprusside testing in urine.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the Haemato-oncology Clinic for review. He presented to his GP with tiredness, night sweats and easy bruising, and has been diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia(AML). He has been unable to work due to disability for the past 2 months. On examination his BP is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular. He looks pale, there is extensive bruising affecting both arms and legs, chest is clear Abdominal examination reveals obvious splenomegaly. Karnovsky score is 65%. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 87 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 26.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 85×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Creatinine 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) 740 U/L 100-190 IU/L Glucose 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 72 mm 0-10 mm in the 1st hour MDR1 Positive Which of the following is the strongest marker of poor prognosis in this patient?
explanation: MDR stands for multidrug resistance, and not surprisingly is associated with poor outcome in patients with AML.

stem: A 51-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has suffered from rheumatoid arthritis for the past 14 years, and is currently treated with methotrexate and etanercept. Her disease is not controlled, she complains of persistent morning stiffness and has obvious small joint polyarthropathy affecting her wrists, ankles, hands and feet on physical examination. Her BP is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. Her chest is clear. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, her BMl is 22. Investigations: You plan to change her medication to rituximab. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of rituximab? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 113 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 59 mm/hr 0-10 mm in the 1st hour
explanation: CD20 is a B-cell receptor, and anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab target the receptor leading to a significant reduction in B-lymphocyte number.In patients with rheumatoid arthritis rituximab has been shown to reduce disease activity in patients who have been resistant to other interventions. Anti- CD20 monoclonal antibodies are also used in the treatment of haematological malignancies.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review with severe pain affecting his right hip. He has a history of sickle cell disease and has suffered from a number of painful crises involving bone pain, and two episodes of acute chest syndrome over the past 2-3 years. He tells you the pain came on all of a sudden and he is now in agony, unable to walk. On examination his BP is 132/80 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular, temperature is 37.9℃. There is localised warmth and erythema over the joint, and flexion and external rotation are severely limited by pain. He has a first litre of IV normal saline running over 1 hour. Which of the following is the most important next intervention?
explanation: Pain control is crucial in the management of vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease, and opiates are usually required. Boluses are usually given on admission to achieve pain control, and over the longer period of inpatient stay patient controlled use of opiates may be valuable.

stem: A 20-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department having taken 40×300 mg aspirin tablets some 1 hour earlier. She is hyperventilating and complaining of ringing in her ears. On examination her BP is 145/80 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. Her respiratory rate is 44. Which of the following would you expect to find with respect to acid-base balance?
explanation: Three stages are well described with respect to acid-base changes associated with salicylate overdose. The first, occurring for the first hours after overdose is associated with a blood pH7.4,urine pH6.0,respiratory alkalosis, and increased urinary excretion of bicarbonate.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with disseminated cervical carcinoma comes to the Emergency Department complaining of worsening pelvic pain. Current medication includes 75 mg of modified release oral morphine twice per day. A recent CT scan has revealed locally advanced disease which was unresponsive to chemotherapy. On examination her BP is 122/82mmHg,pulse is 82/min and regular. She is complaining of deep-seated aching pain, not relieved by her current morphine dose. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her breakthrough pain? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 167×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145μmol/L(130 some 3 months earlier) 50-120 μmol/l
explanation: Although this patient has mild renal impairment, she is well established on oral morphine. As such in this situation the optimal next step is to allow PRN use of morphine elixir until pain is controlled. This can then be converted to an increased dose of MST or to an alternative route of opiate delivery such as buprenorphine patches.

stem: A35-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with recurrent episodes of pneumonia over the past 4 years requiring multiple courses of antibiotics. He has a history of whooping cough as a child and smoked for 3 years between the ages of 16 and 19. His GP prescribed a salbutamol inhaler for shortness of breath, although he maintains it did not make much difference to his symptoms. On examination his BP is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular. He is apyrexial. There are coarse crackles on auscultation at both lung bases. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count WCC 10.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 61 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Chest X-ray Patchy shadowing affecting both lung bases Which of the following would you expect to find on high-resolution CT scanning of the chest?
options: Linear bands of fibrosis radiating from the hila
Reduced bronchial diameter vs corresponding vascular bundle
explanation: This is used to describe multi centrilobular nodules with a linear branching pattern connecting them.Other features of bronchiectasis include bronchial dilatation and lack of bronchial tapering moving from proximal to distal regions of the lung.

stem: A 62-year-old man is discharged from the medical ward having been admitted with uncontrolled atrial fibrillation. He has a history of COPD for which he takes high dose seretide and PRN salbutamol, and symptoms of heart failure which precipitated his admission have been stabilised with the use of ramipril, furosemide and bisoprolol. On examination his BP is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 65/min (atrial fibrillation). He has minor crackles at both bases on auscultation and pitting oedema of his ankles which has improved significantly since his admission. Investigations:
explanation: Rivaroxaban is a direct inhibitor of factor Xa, inhibiting both thrombin formation and development of thrombi. Rivaroxaban does not inhibit the action of thrombin itself (activated factor I) and no effects on platelets have been demonstrated.

stem: A 61-year-old man with presents to the clinic with increasing weakness, so that he is finding it very difficult to climb the stairs, and to get out of low chairs in his lounge. He has a chronic cough which has been present for at least 2 years, and he smokes 20 cigarettes per day. On examination is BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Auscultation of the chest reveals bilateral poor air entry and quiet wheeze. Abdomen is soft and non-tender,his BMI is 23. He has proximal weakness affecting his shoulders and hips, and some weakness of grip strength which improves with repetition. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 114 g/l 135-175g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 115μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 75 mm/hr 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Chest X-ray Changes consistent with COPD and a left hilar mass Which of the following antibodies is most likely found in association with his muscle weakness?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is Lambert—Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), as evidenced by proximal myopathy, where strength is improved by repeated movement, and likely underlying bronchial carcinoma. Anti-VGCC antibodies result in a loss of function of voltage-gated calcium channels at motor nerve terminals.

stem: A 26-year-old man, who has returned from his honeymoon in the Dominican Republic one week earlier, comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has suffered from fevers and lethargy over the past few days and has significant pain affecting his right knee, left ankle and right foot. He also has conjunctivitis and a rash affecting both feet. On further questioning it transpires he had a food poisoning illness whilst he was away which resolved spontaneously over a few days. A family history of psoriatic arthritis is noted. On examination his BP is 110/70mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular, temperature is 37.6℃.Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal systems are unremarkable. You confirm oligoarthritis with mild swelling and limitation of movement. A psoriatic-type rash is affecting both feet and his hands. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 10.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate(ESR) 70 mm 0-10 mm in the 1st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 150 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: The history here is suggestive of possible reactive arthritis related to the Gl infection whilst on holiday. Symptoms usually follow some 2-4 weeks after the initial infective episode, and are characterised by oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis, and other features including keratoderma blennorrhagica, and urethritis when the arthritis follows an episode of sexually transmitted infection. Non-steroidals are the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a throbbing headache which is worse in the morning and last thing at night. She says that the headache has increased significantly in intensity over the past few weeks and is made worse by coughing and straining, and improved by standing up. Despite taking regular paracetamol and ibuprofen it has not improved. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her BP is 155/90 mmHg,pulse is 72/min and regular. There is no focal neurological deficit. Her BMI is 35. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L 7 mmol/L CT head Normal size ventricles, no focal lesion identified Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In an obese female with morning and evening headaches suggestive of raised intracranial pressure, papilloedema, and a history of oral contraceptive pill use, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is the diagnosis until proven otherwise. Lumbar puncture with pressure measurement, to confirm the diagnosis, is the next most appropriate step.

stem: A19-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with her mother. She has suffered from gradual weight loss over the past few months, and according to her mother has not been eating at all. She is thought to have lost 10kg in weight overall. She takes no regular medication and has not had a menstrual period for the past 4 months. On examination her BP is 100/60mmHg, pulse is 62/min and regular. She is pale. Heart sounds are normal. Chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender, her BMI is 17.0.Her arms and legs are covered in fine lanugo hair. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 200×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L* Which of the following is also likely to be found?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis here, with decreased BMI, amenorrhoea, lanugo hair and hypokalaemia, is anorexia nervosa. As such elevated cortisol is usually seen as part of a stress response.

stem: A35-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disease is admitted to the Emergency Department following an overdose of lithium. She took an unknown number of tablets and was found by her partner some 3-4 hours after taking the overdose. On examination in the Emergency Department her GCS is 9. Her BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 95/min and regular. There is increased tone bilaterally and hyperreflexia. She suffers a brief tonic clonic seizure during your initial physical examination. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 199×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 141μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/l Lithium 5.8 mmol/L 0.4-1.2 mmol/L Which of the following is the optimal way to manage her lithium overdose?
explanation: Given this patient has a severe lithium overdose(level greater than 4.0 mmol/l) with symptoms, haemodialysis is the most appropriate intervention. Lithium is low molecular weight, has negligible protein binding and a small volume of distribution. This makes it highly amenable to haemodialysis.

stem: A 21-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department having fainted at work. He feels that he never has any energy, having always struggled with sport at school, he takes no regular exercise. He takes no regular medication and has no significant past medical history. On examination his BP is 100/80mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. General physical assessment is normal, his BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 200×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO) 31 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/l Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Where is the most likely underlying pathological lesion?
explanation: Gitelman Syndrome explanations The most likely diagnosis here is Gitelman's syndrome, which causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.The syndrome occurs because of loss-of-function mutations of the thiazide-sensitive sodiumchloride symporter, which is situated in the distal convoluted tubule. Potassium supplementation and potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone are both potential interventions.

stem: A29-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with problems with the vision in her left eye over the past 12 hours. She tells you that she has lost colour vision in the eye, and is now suffering from light flashes affecting her acuity, and fading out of her sight in that eye. She is also complaining of pain behind the eye which is worse on movement. There is no past medical history of note and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On arrival in the department she is clearly distressed, her BP is 122/80mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular.Her visual acuity is reduced at 6/36 from normal in the left eye and there is decreased pupillary light reaction on the left. The macula and retina appear normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: ADON presents in this manner, with gradually deteriorating vision, often with loss of colour vision first, followed by decreasing acuity and light flashes across the visual field. Focal defects may also be seen. The patient's age and lack of past medical history also support a diagnosis of ADON versus other options.

stem: A 20-year-old female rugby player comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a rash affecting her lower abdomen, inner thighs and genital region. She tells you that the lesions are mostly asymptomatic, although the occasional one becomes sore or itchy. A photograph of the lesions is shown below: Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: External Links Interventions for cutaneous mollusc⋯ ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19821333?do... This rash is consistent with molluscum contagiosum, caused by MCV1,a DNA pox virus. In adults it is spread by close contact, which can include sharing baths, towels, flannels etc. It is likely that spread in the rugby changing room has occurred. No specific intervention is required and the lesions resolve spontaneously over the course of a few months. Molluscum Contagiosum explanations AHIV testing HIV testing is incorrect. Larger lesions(up to 15mm) and more extensive spread, is usually seen in HIV, and we are not given any risk factors for HIV infection in the scenario.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the Neurology Clinic for review. He is extremely worried as his brother who is 28 years old has begun to develop symptoms of mood disturbance. Apparently their father presented with similar symptoms at the age of 42, and was later diagnosed with Huntington's disease. Their grandmother committed suicide at the age of 58 with similar neurological symptoms. Which of the following describes earlier presentation of Huntington's with successive generations?
explanation: Huntington's shows genetic anticipation where symptoms become more severe and presentation occurs at an earlier age with successive generations.This is because of expansion of the trinucleotide repeat sequence which is the root cause of Huntington's.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic for review. He has suffered increasing weakness affecting his facial muscles and upper arms, which began affecting only the the face some 3-4 years ago. He has chronic pain affecting his upper back and shoulders, and mild high-tone deafness which he puts down to his hobby of shooting. On examination there is evidence of bilateral facial weakness, winging of both scapulae and forward movement of the medial end of both clavicles when the arms are abducted. There is pectoral wasting but the deltoids are relatively spared. Blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 78/min and regular. There are no heart murmurs. Chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged FMD presents with this classical picture of facial weakness occurring first,followed by weakness of the shoulder muscles, but with relative preservation of deltoid function. It occurs because of inappropriate expression of the DU×4 gene which leads to muscle cell death. High-tone deafness, retinal changes and cardiac arrhythmias are also seen.

stem: A51-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with hyperpigmentation affecting his armpits, groin and the folds on the back of his neck. He has lost 4kg in weight over the past 5 weeks, and tells you that he is generally off his food, with intermittent nausea and fullness after meals. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has a history of COPD for which he takes high-dose seretide BD. On examination his BP is 155/82 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular. There is wheeze bilaterally on auscultation, consistent with his underlying COPD. Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the epigastrium. You can see a velvety hyperpigmented rash, particularly prominent over both axillae. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 94 g/l 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 7.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L* Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) 95 IU/L 10-40 IU/L Alkaline Phosphatase 95 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 12 μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The rash is most consistent with a diagnosis of acanthosis nigricans, and in the case of malignancy- associated acanthosis nigricans, 90% of cases are thought to be related to underlying gastric cancer. The weight loss over the past few weeks, symptoms of early fullness after a meal, anaemia and elevated transaminases would also be consistent with the diagnosis.

stem: A 42-year-old man who runs a pub comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. It transpires his main problem is polyuria most evenings, towards the end of a stint at the bar. On further questioning he tells you that he drinks up to six pints of beer each evening. Which of the following is the primary cause of polyuria associated with binge alcohol consumption?
explanation: During the acute phase of alcohol consumption, ethanol is recognised to reduce ADH release from the posterior pituitary. This is thought to account for polyuria related to binging on alcohol. Chronic effects on ADH receptors in the CNS may also mediate production of corticotrophin releasing factor, mood, depression and risk-taking behaviour with reduced ADH activity in the CNS known to impact on psychological wellbeing.

stem: A35-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an indurated erythematous red/purple rash on both shins. He says this has developed over the past 4 months and has become increasingly noticeable. He also complains of increasing lethargy and listlessness, and intermittent diarrhoea and abdominal pain, which his GP has put down to irritable bowel syndrome. On examination his BP is 115/80mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. He looks pale. Abdomen is soft and non-tender,his BM is 22.PR and rigid sigmoidoscopy are unremarkable. There is a nodular rash affecting both shins. You also notice ridging of his finger nails. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/L 135-175 g/L Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 104 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 179×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 29 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Albumin 35 g/l 35-55 g/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 65 mm/hr 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The presence of erythema nodosum and Gl symptoms implies inflammatory bowel disease. Anaemia with raised MCV and nail ridging implies B vitamin deficiency, which in this case is potentially due to small bowel inflammation. This makes Crohn's more likely than ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with headaches that have been steadily worsening over the past 3 months. She describes the headaches as dull and giving her a sickening feeling, saying they are worse in the morning and late at night, are associated with nausea, and made worse by lying down. She also tells you that when she bends forward to pick up something off the floor, there is greying out of her vision. Past medical history of note includes obesity and impaired glucose tolerance, for which she is under GP follow-up. On examination her BP is 155/85mmHg, pulse is 67/min and regular.Her body mass index is 35. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 127 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 198×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 6.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L CT head No focal lesion MR venogram No sign of venous thrombosis Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The evidence presented (postural headaches, visual changes in an obese individual, coupled with unremarkable CT and MR venogram) raises the possibility idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Most evidence supports the use of acetazolamide, which has been shown in clinical trials to reduce the degree of papilloedema and to impact on symptoms including headache and visual disturbance.

stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She presented to her GP for routine blood testing after moving house, and was found to have a mildly elevated calcium at 2.85 mmol/L. She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. On examination her BP is 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular. There are no significant physical findings. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 89μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca+) 2.85 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/l Albumin 40 g/l 35-55 g/L Ca/Cr clearance ratio Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: The clinical picture as described here is most consistent with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia(FHH), which is an entirely benign condition. It is an autosomal dominant condition resulting from an inactivating mutation in the gene coding for the calcium-sensing receptor. No intervention is required.

stem: A45-year-old woman presents to the transplant clinic with worsening diarrhoea over the past few weeks. She had a renal transplant some 5 months ago and has taken immunosuppressive therapy since then. Current drug treatment includes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, low-dose prednisolone, ramipril and indapamide for blood pressure control. On examination her BP is 126/82 mmHg,pulse is 70/min and regular. There is mild left-sided tenderness on abdominal palpation, her renal transplant scar is healing well. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 184×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 139 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: Diarrhoea is common after transplantation, and in the case of drug-induced diarrhoea,50% of cases are thought to be due to mycophenolate mofetil. It is recognised to cause an ulcerating colitis, which usually resolves after dose reduction or cessation of mycophenolate therapy. In those cases where it does not resolve, response to anti-TNF biological therapy is seen.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic with hypertension and persistent proteinuria. Her GP is currently managing her with lisinopril and indapamide but she is still hypertensive. She recalls having a number of urinary tract infections when she was very young, but has no other past medical history of note. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, there are no renal masses. BMl is 22.5. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 154 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Urine blood protein USS renal tract Bilateral irregularly shrunken kidneys Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The history of recurrent urinary tract infections in childhood, coupled with hypertension and proteinuria, against a background of irregularly scarred kidneys, is typical of reflux nephropathy. To prevent reflux nephropathy, urinary tract infection in children is now aggressively investigated, particularly to rule out vesicoureteric reflux,and treatment with antibiotics is instigated early.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department having collapsed whilst praying at the local church.According to her husband she has recently been prescribed a course of erythromycin by her GP for a respiratory tract infection. On examination her BP is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear.You note spells of torsades de pointes VT on her monitor. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Magnesium 0.6 mmol/L 0.75-1.0 mmol/L Calcium 2.2 mmol/l 2.2-2.6 mmol/L ECG (during period of sinus rhythm) QT prolongation at 505 ms Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This woman has acquired long-QT as a result of erythromycin therapy, which has led to episodes of torsades de pointes VT. In addition to discontinuing the erythromycin, magnesium is the intervention of choice. Even as here in the face of normal magnesium levels, IV magnesium has been proven to reduce the frequency of further arrhythmias.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of acute arthritic pain affecting his right knee, which is severely limiting movement. He has a history of renal impairment thought to be due to chronic hypertension, and he takes lisinopril, bisoprolol and indapamide. On examination his BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 68/min and regular. Heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. Abdomen is soft and non-tender and his BMI is 25. His right knee is swollen and erythematous, and his flexion is limited to 30 degrees. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/L 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 182μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urate 0.35 mmol/L 0.1-0.4 mmol/L X-ray of both knees Evidence of chondrocalcinosis Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Like gout, acute flares of pseudogout(the most likely diagnosis here) respond to intervention with colchicine.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia. Her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill, and she has a history of irritable bowel syndrome over the past 6-9 months. Her periods are monthly and light. Her father died of colon cancer at the age of 67.On examination her BP is 107/80mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. She looks pale. There are no cardiovascular or respiratory findings of note. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, her BMI is 22.5. Investigations (after 4 weeks of FeSO4): Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 97 g/l 115-155 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 77 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium 2.1 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Albumin 32 g/l 35-55 g/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 23 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Bilirubin 11μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: In this situation, with iron deficiency anaemia which is poorly responsive to oral iron supplements, unexplained irritable bowel syndrome symptoms, and a calcium at the lower end of the normal range, coeliac disease should be considered. In women of child-bearing age who do not respond to initial iron replacement, TTG antibody testing is recommended as the next step in investigations.

stem: You review a 72-year-old man who has suffered a basilar artery territory stroke. He appears to have developed a homonymous hemianopia, verbal dyslexia, and a memory defect indicating interruption of the cortical branches of the posterior cerebral artery. Where is the origin of the posterior cerebral artery?
options: Near to the origin of the anterior choroidal artery
Near the intersection with the posterior communicating artery
Near the origin of the basilar artery
Posterior to the origin of the superior cerebellar artery
Posterior to the origin of the pontine arteries
explanation: The posterior cerebral artery arises near the intersection of the posterior communicating artery and the basilar artery and connects with the ipsilateral middle cerebral artery and internal carotid artery via the posterior communicating artery. Interruption in the blood supply occurs via the cortical branches of the posterior cerebral artery.

stem: You are investigating accumulation of a peptide associated with early onset dementia in three families who are followed up in your local neurology unit. What is the most appropriate way to characterise the amino acid sequence of the peptide?
explanation: Western blotting uses gel electrophoresis to separate native proteins by 3-D structure or denatured proteins by the length of the polypeptide. The proteins are transferred to a membrane, where they are stained with antibodies specific to the target protein.

stem: A 69-year-old man with a history of COPD is admitted to the Emergency Department having suffered an acute stroke. He awoke from sleep with a dense right-sided hemiparesis and his partner immediately called an ambulance. Other past history of note includes hypertension for which he receives indapamide and lisinopril. On examination his BP is 185/100 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular.Chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender. He has a dense right-sided hemiparesis affecting the face, arm and leg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 220 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 620×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 152μmol/L 50-120 μmol Viscosity CT head No signs of haemorrhage Which of the following is the initial treatment of choice?
explanation: This patient most likely has underlying primary polycythaemia, leading to a thrombotic stroke. Although interventions may be considered over the longer term to manage both haemoglobin and platelet count, the acute-phase management is the same as for other patients presenting with an acute stroke.

stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has suffered from five exacerbations of asthma over the past year which have required a course of oral corticosteroids. Other medication includes high-dose salmeterol/fluticasone combination inhaler, and daily montelukast. On examination her BP is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular. There is bilateral polyphonic wheeze on auscultation of her chest. Peak flow is 340L(510 predicted).Blood testing reveals an elevated total IgE. Patch testing has revealed allergies to trees, grasses, fungus and moulds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Omalizumab is anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, which is indicated for patients with severe allergic asthma who have required more than four courses of oral corticosteroids over the past year. In this case potential risks of anaphylaxis, and impairment of immune surveillance, are outweighed by the risks of frequent high-dose systemic corticosteroids.

stem: A 35-year-old man who was diagnosed HIV positive some 3 years earlier, but lost to follow up, presents to the clinic with multiple red/purple skin lesions, including within the mouth. He tells you they have developed gradually over the past few months. An image of the rash is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: The rash shown here is typical of Kaposi's sarcoma, with multiple highly vascular lesions. Introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy(HAART) leads to a reduction in lesions in 40% of patients who take it. In those who do not see an improvement in their lesions, systemic therapies include interferon alpha, liposomal anthracyclines and paclitaxel.

stem: A50-year-old man is referred to the acute medical take with worsening night-time fevers,right upper quadrant pain and abnormal liver function tests. He had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy some 10 weeks earlier and has been taking no other medication apart from analgesia since then. On examination his BP is 115/80 mmHg, pulse is 77min and regular. Temperature is 37.9°℃. Heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. Abdomen is soft, but there is marked tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 122×10/L 150-400×10/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 289 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l CT abdomen Evidence of a collection in the right lobe of the liver Blood cultures (sent 2 days ago by GP) Streptococcus millerigrown in both bottles Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
explanation: Antibiotics including Mode of Action explanations Members of the Streptococcus anginosus group (of which S. milleri is one) are sensitive to ceftriaxone, and this is therefore the antibiotic intervention of choice. It is also very common to see co-existent infection with anaerobic organisms, and coverage with metronidazole for these is required.

stem: A 17-year-old man comes to the Nephrology Clinic with his parents. Over the past 2-3 weeks he has suffered from progressive swelling of both lower limbs and peri-orbital oedema. He apparently suffered from a similar episode some 3 years earlier, which resolved after a course of corticosteroid therapy. On examination his BP is 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular.You confirm facial oedema and pitting oedema affecting both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets 199×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Glucose 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Protein 3.8 g/24 hours 60-80 g/L Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: The history of recurrent oedema, coupled with resolution after a course of corticosteroids, fits well with a diagnosis of minimal change disease. Although hypertension is rare in children, it is seen slightly more commonly in adults, as is a mild elevation in creatinine. Corticosteroids are effective in 90% of adults with the condition, although the response may be delayed in adults versus children (16 versus 6 weeks).

stem: A 60-year-old demolition worker comes to the Respiratory Clinic with progressive shortness of breath over the past year. This has failed to improve despite salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers, and he is now finding it difficult to walk his dog. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day and drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. On examination his BP is 122/80 mmHg,pulse is 78/min and regular. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest and bilateral inspiratory crackles. There is bilateral pitting oedema affecting both ankles and examination of the hands reveals clubbing. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50-120μmol/L Chest X-ray Bilateral pleural plaques, patchy bilateral shadowing Forced Expiratory Volume in the 1st second (FEV1) 2.8l(predicted 3.47) 4.5-3.5l Forced vital capacity (FVC) 3.4l(predicted 4.59) 4.5-3.5L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The symptoms of gradually worsening shortness of breath, coupled with changes consistent with asbestos exposure and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing(20% reduction in both FEV1 and FVC), fit best with asbestos-related lung fibrosis. It is likely given his work as a demolition worker that he has been exposed to asbestos in his job.

stem: 8 1):YV yLA(cb.jxl A45-year-old rough sleeper who has been diagnosed with tuberculosis presents to the Emergency Department some 4 weeks into treatment with his antituberculous medication. He is unable to mobilise because of acute arthritis affecting his left great toe. Current medication includes isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin and ethambutol. He is also now taking telmisartan for management of hypertension. On examination in the Emergency Department he is clearly in significant pain, his BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 89/min and regular. There is obvious erythema, swelling and restricted movement affecting the left big toe. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urate 0.55 mmol/L 0.1-0.4 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely medication to have caused his acute gout?
explanation: Pyrazinamide reduces uric acid excretion by approximately 80% at the therapeutic dose of 300 mg per day. Pyrazinoic acid, the metabolite of pyrazinamide, is oxidised by xanthine oxidase, which may be responsible for the hyperuricaemic effect of therapy. Between 40% and 100% of patients treated with pyrazinamide are found to have uric acid levels above the upper limit of normal.

stem: A71-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic because of a rise in her serum creatinine from 135 μmol/l to 160 μmol/l since last measured 3 months earlier. She takes a number of medications for hypertension, diabetes and reflux oesophagitis, and has suffered from a recent urinary tract infection. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Her blood pressure is 134/82mmHg,pulse is 74/min and regular. Her chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no peripheral oedema. Which of the following medications is most likely to be the cause of the rise in creatinine?
explanation: Trimethoprim is the agent most recognised to block creatinine secretion resulting in a 35-44μmol/L increase in serum creatinine without actually affecting GFR. It is thought to compete with creatinine for the organic cation secretory pump.

stem: A49-year-old man who has spent some time teaching in Southeast Asia presents to the Emergency Department with a severe fever, headache and joint pains. He is suspected to have infection with Plasmodium vivax. Which one life-cycle stage occurs in P.vivax but not in P.falciparum infection?
explanation: Hypnozoites represent the “dormant” Lliver stage of the life-cycle of P.vivaxand P.ovale infection (i.e. benign malarias), and can cause late relapses after treatment. To eradicate hypnozoites and prevent such relapses, a course of primaquine must be given following chloroquine therapy for P.vivaxand P.ovale infection. They are not part of the life-cycle of P.falciparum,for this reason primaquine is not required after quinine therapy.

stem: A 65-year-old man who is admitted to hospital for right-sided pneumonia becomes acutely confused and aggressive on the ward. He is known to drink 3 pints of beer per day. He lives alone andis independent with respect to all his needs. When you see him he has pulled out his drip and he is trying to punch the nursing and medical staff suggesting that they are all out to kill him. You calm him down temporarily and examine him. On examination he is pyrexial 38.2℃, has a BP of 100/60 mmHg and a pulse of 92/min, regular. There are signs of extensive right-sided consolidation on respiratory examination. Limited neurological examination reveals no gaze palsy, and marked ataxia appears absent. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 108 g/l 135-175 g/L Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 102 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count(WCC) 13.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 136 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 180 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Acute confusional state secondary to infection
explanation: While there is evidence of alcohol consumption here, this patient has significant signs of acute infection, with a pyrexia, hypotension and tachycardia, raised white count and renal impairment. As such the major contributor to his symptoms is more likely to be his lower respiratory tract infection; significant hypoxia should also be ruled out as a contributor. Management of this patient should include removing as many stimuli, which are likely to worsen his agitation,as possible, including nursing him in an adequately lit room, away from other patients if possible, and making sure that a stable team of nurses who he recognises are able to look after him .In view of his pneumonia, use of sedation should be avoided as this may worsen any hypoxia and make him more confused and agitated.

stem: A20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 36 hours after an overdose of 40×500 mg paracetamol tablets. She now regrets the overdose and is feeling increasingly unwell with nausea. There is no past medical history of note and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 88/min and regular. She is tender over the right upper quadrant of her abdomen and there is mild jaundice. Investigations: Which of the findings drives referral to a specialist liver unit? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 142×10/L 150-400×109/L Prothrombin Time (PT) 36s 10.6-14.9 s Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT) 32.1 s 23.0-35.0 s Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 142 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L* Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 1579 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Bilirubin 32μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Albumin 31 g/l 35-55 g/L AALT 1579
explanation: INR is above 2.0(upper limit of normal for PT is 14) within 48 hours of the paracetamol overdose. This fulfils a criterion for referral to a specialist liver unit, as synthetic liver function is likely to deteriorate further. Other factors which drive specialist referral include: · Renal impairment(creatinine200 μmol/L) ·Systolic BP80 mm Hg despite adequate fluid resuscitation · Hypoglycaemia · Metabolic acidosis(pH7.3 or bicarbonate18 mmol/L).

stem: A 17-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has a history of cystic fibrosis but has remained relatively well with only one admission for pneumonia over the past year. Over the past 3 months she has noticed increased shortness of breath and sputum production, and her most recent sample has proved positive for Pseudomonas. On examination her BP is 123/82 mmHg, pulse is 76/min and regular. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation, more marked at the bases. PEFR is reduced at 300 L(dropped from 380 lsome 3 months earlier). Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for Pseudomonas eradication?
explanation: Modern management of cystic fibrosis dictates that if possible Pseudomonas should be eradicated as soon as possible after first colonisation. Out of regimens tested, nebulised tobramycin was most effective when compared with ciprofloxacin, and there was no benefit of adding ciprofloxacin to tobramycin therapy. More than 90% of patients become Pseudomonas free after 28-day course of therapy.

stem: You are consenting a 19-year-old man, who is thought to have a congenital neurological degenerative disorder,for collection of genetic material. He tells you he has heard about the Human Genome Project. Which one of the following statements is true concerning the project?
options: Alu repeats were identified and are thought to be “junk”
10,000 full-length human cDNAs have been identified
3.7 million human single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been mapped
95% of the gene-containing part of the human DNA sequence has been examined
explanation: 3.7 million human single nucleotide polymorphisms(SNPs) have been mapped as part of the Human Genome Project and are available for gene association studies.
